findings.text: The opening says plainly what Athena is and why this page exists, so a newcomer can say what they are looking at in two sentences.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: This URL is Athena's home page, but the page is almost entirely about another project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to infer from one lede sentence that the study is meant as a demonstration, and gets no direct account of how to use Athena itself.
There is a clear next action for both projects and for checking a claim. But it sits near the bottom, after the full study, where a newcomer who only wants Athena may not scroll.
findings.source: Next steps: "Learn about Athena, and how to install and try it: https://github.com/doodla/athena"

findings.text: The identifier `firstmate-work-handling` appears without any explanation of what it names. To a newcomer it is noise.
findings.source: "This page is that study of firstmate, from firstmate-work-handling."

findings.text: "Yolo", "captain" and "local-only landing" appear in the very first section with no definition there. The glossary defines yolo and captain much further down, and it never defines "local-only landing".
findings.source: Start here: "With the yolo setting off, the captain approves every PR merge and every local-only landing."

findings.text: The page cites transitions t1 and t3 before the Transitions section has defined them. A first-time reader meets ids that mean nothing yet.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3"

findings.text: The design-choice cards are titled only with opaque ids, so a reader skimming them can't tell what each one is about without reading its body.
findings.source: Why it is built this way: card headings "ra1", "ra2", "ra3", "ra4"

findings.text: The page uses "home" as a term, here and in claims c1 and c15, but never defines it.
findings.source: Glossary: "A unit of work in a home's backlog. Dispatch refuses an item the home does not have."

findings.text: This limit is about Athena's internal data format. A newcomer will find it confusing, though the page is honest about it.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f2: "The study's data format asks every guard to name who checks it, and it has no way to say nobody does, so these transitions name the agent as a stand-in."

findings.text: Some claims list the same source link twice, which looks careless to a reader checking sources.
findings.source: Claims and sources, c2 and c14: the same link, e.g. "docs/configuration.md:357-357", listed twice

findings.text: The Start here section, together with the numbered walkthrough of one task, gives a clear and readable path through firstmate. Every statement is cited, which supports the page's point about traceability.
findings.source: Start here: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails or has no limit."
